item.title: U.S. debt blows past $40 trillion, jeopardizing quality of life for every American
item.description: The U.S. national debt surpassed $40 trillion, nearly $300,000 per household, as the debt-to-GDP ratio hits 124% with few solutions in sight.
item.content:encoded:
America’s national debt is climbing higher with few solutions in sight. Total public debt outstanding exceeded $40 trillion for the first time in history — that's nearly $300,000 per household. This figure should alarm every American, yet years of political promises of easy fixes have dulled the public’s sense of urgency.

As America races past the grim, $40-trillion milestone, it is essential to confront why such a high debt is an existential threat to our republic and what realistic solutions remain.

The most common benchmark is the debt-to-GDP ratio. Total U.S. public debt now exceeds 124% of GDP. Only a handful of countries rank worse — among them Sudan, Venezuela, and stagnant developed economies like Japan, Greece and Italy.

$50 TRILLION IN DEBT IS NOT A DISTANT THREAT. AMERICA IS SPEEDING TOWARDS IT

No country should aspire to rank among the highest in this metric, yet America does.

Even debt held by the public, over $32 trillion, stands near 100% of GDP. And according to the Congressional Budget Office, it's projected to reach 120% by 2036.

TRUMP INTERVENES AS HOUSE GOP REVOLT PUTS SAVE AMERICA ACT AT CENTER OF SPENDING SHOWDOWN

A rising debt-to-GDP ratio signals America’s eroding capacity to service existing obligations without heavy reliance on borrowing. Overwhelming national debt slows economic growth, puts upward pressure on inflation and interest rates, reduces investor confidence, diminishes the American dollar’s standing as the global currency and may even spur a fiscal crisis.

These aren't just theoretical risks — exorbitant debt produces concrete economic damage. One outcome is the crowding-out effect. Here’s how it works:

TOP JPMORGANCHASE EXEC WARNS REGULATORY PROPOSAL COULD SQUEEZE CREDIT FOR MILLIONS OF SMALL BUSINESSES

The government borrows to pay back debt obligations. It does so by selling bonds to finance deficits. This reduces the supply of available funds in the market. The result is upward pressure on interest rates and less capital for private investment. This makes it more difficult for businesses to borrow and invest in job creation, innovation and expansion or for individuals to take out loans.

In short, more debt means less free-flowing money in the economy.

The Congressional Budget Office estimates that for every dollar the deficit increases, private investment falls by 33 cents. Still more, an additional $1 trillion in debt reduces long-run U.S. capital stock of productive assets by 0.7-0.8%. More government debt means less private capital formation, slower productivity growth, and, ultimately, less money in the pockets of Americans.

These effects are quiet but damaging. Unlike sudden shocks to the economy — trade disruptions, technological developments or global conflicts — the debt compounds over time. It’s a handy tool for politicians to paper over today’s problems with massive amounts of spending while shifting the burden to future generations.

JOHN ADAMS MADE A TERRIFYING PREDICTION. AMERICA IS CLOSE TO PROVING HIM CORRECT

Some politicians have absurdly denied the danger of the debt, instead convincing the public that America can spend without limit. The theory undergirding that argument is Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) and has been advocated by Democrat New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Vermont Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders’s top economist.

They argue that an issuer of fiat currency as powerful as the United States can always spend its way out of crisis. Yet they disregard crowding-out effects, the erosion of consumer confidence and the fact that currency ultimately rests on real economic value. Treating the dollar as unlimited political fuel is a sure path to runaway inflation and a loss of fiscal credibility.

Prudent economic policy means confronting sustained levels of deficit spending and high national debt before the two grow further out of control. Net interest costs have already surpassed $1 trillion annually and are projected to climb sharply, reaching more than $2 trillion within a decade and consuming a greater share of federal revenues.

The straightforward solution is to eliminate federal deficits and balance the budget. Recent data records a $1.8 trillion deficit in 2025. The government must instead run a surplus and begin repaying its outstanding debt obligations.

Restraining spending growth — particularly in major entitlement programs driving long-term imbalances — and unleashing the American economy via policies that expand the productive private sector are essential. Incremental efficiency efforts, including state-level DOGE reform, help at the margin, but structural reform is necessary to ensure a sustainable budget.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Both parties spent the United States into this $40 trillion mess, so it is the bipartisan responsibility of lawmakers to commit themselves to decisive fiscal action now. Inaction guarantees higher interest payments, reduced private investment, diminished fiscal flexibility in times of crisis and a heavier tax or inflation burden on future generations.

The clock is ticking, and the choice is simple: Act now or mortgage America's future.

Michael Bicksel is a former member of the Heritage Foundation’s Young Leaders Program.

item.title: Meghan Markle's acting U-turn exposes 'lingering problem' after six years of reinventions: experts
item.description: Meghan Markle remains in talks to join "The Gentlemen" Season 3, raising questions about six years of post-royal reinvention.
item.content:encoded:
Meghan Markle spent years trying to reinvent herself after leaving royal life — but her latest move could bring her right back to where she started.

With Season 3 of "The Gentlemen" officially greenlit, the Duchess of Sussex remains in talks to join Guy Ritchie's hit drama, People magazine reported, contradicting earlier reports that the potential deal had fallen through. No deal has been finalized, the outlet said.

"If she returns now, it raises the obvious question — what happened to all those other identities she tried on after leaving royal life?" Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube's "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital.

MEGHAN MARKLE’S ACTING RETURN COULD SPARK FRESH PROBLEMS WITH PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON: EXPERT

"Podcaster, producer, lifestyle entrepreneur, philanthropist, media mogul," said Schofield. "Returning to acting would suggest that the most viable professional identity Meghan has found may ultimately be the one she walked away from."

The talks are in "very early stages," Deadline previously reported. It’s unclear how many episodes she would appear in. The series, which stars Theo James, Kaya Scodelario and Giancarlo Esposito, is filmed in the U.K. and set in England.

Meghan has already dipped her toe back into acting. In 2025, she filmed a small cameo as herself in Amazon MGM Studios' upcoming comedy "Close Personal Friends," starring Brie Larson, Lily Collins, Jack Quaid and Henry Golding. The potential role in "The Gentlemen," however, would mark a more significant return to scripted acting after leaving "Suits."

WATCH: MEGHAN MARKLE COULD REVIVE CAREER WITH SHOCKING ACTING RETURN: EXPERT

"The Gentlemen" follows Eddie Horniman (Theo James), who unexpectedly inherits his father’s title as Duke of Halstead and the family’s sprawling estate after his father dies — only to discover that Halstead Manor sits atop a massive cannabis operation and that his reckless older brother has been passed over.

Doug Eldridge, founder of Achilles PR, told Fox News Digital that Meghan's potential Hollywood comeback could expose the challenge that has followed her for years: finding an identity once the camera stops rolling that sticks.

"This has been the lingering problem for Meghan all these years: what is her identity?" he said. "She's ridden a carousel of career horses. Yet for all the rotations, nothing has seemingly stuck."

In a statement shared with The New York Times, a spokesperson for the Sussexes said, "On the heels of a wonderful trip with family and friends this summer, Harry and Meghan have decided to spend an extended period in the U.K. this autumn. They are excited to have their children spend more time in the country that’s such an important part of their family’s story."

The spokesperson confirmed that the couple's business operations will remain based in the U.S. Meghan and Harry will also keep their California home. People magazine reported that Meghan's potential acting project contributed to the couple's decision to return to Britain.

Schofield isn't convinced that filmmakers will now embrace Meghan with open arms.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"I'm still skeptical that this represents some grand Hollywood comeback," she said.

"Meghan has spent six years in [California] with a multimillion-dollar Netflix relationship, enormous name recognition and Tyler Perry on speed dial. If acting was genuinely her ambition, she was already standing in arguably the best place in the world to pursue it."

"That said, 'The Gentlemen' would be a clever choice," she noted. "It's an established hit with a strong creative pedigree, so she wouldn't have to carry the project herself. But first, she has to prove she can disappear into a character rather than have every scene become about Meghan Markle."

In 2022, when asked by Variety whether she would ever return to acting, Meghan replied: "I’m done."

"I guess never say never, but my intention is to absolutely not," she said at the time.

Since stepping back from royal duties in 2020, Meghan has launched a series of ventures with mixed results. 

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Her high-profile Spotify partnership ended in 2023 after her podcast, "Archetypes," produced one season. Her planned Netflix animated series "Pearl" was scrapped before reaching production.

Her lifestyle brand, originally launched as American Riviera Orchard, endured a prolonged rollout before being relaunched to As Ever in 2025. In March 2026, a Sussex spokesperson confirmed that her Netflix lifestyle series, "With Love, Meghan," would continue as seasonal specials rather than return for a third season.

Dan Wakeford, founder of Celebrity Intelligence, told Fox News Digital that after years of reinvention, Meghan may have little to lose by returning to the career that first put her in the spotlight.

"The honest picture is more complicated than any of the tabloid headlines and narratives about the empire," he explained. "'With Love, Meghan' became a punchline when it needed to be a launchpad. And when the show was mocked, it poisoned the well for As Ever as well, because the credibility was gone. The problem is that she and Harry believed the big Netflix deals and Spotify checks meant they had leverage when, actually, the checks were the leverage."

"The most interesting path forward for Meghan, and several sources raised this unprompted to Celebrity Intelligence, is a return to acting would actually be a wise move," he continued. "Find an extraordinary script the way Demi Moore did with 'The Substance' and do something that shocks people. Get away from this princess arc and go back to what you loved and what made you famous in the first place."

Meghan, daughter of Emmy-winning lighting director Thomas Markle, got her start in Hollywood with bit parts on shows like "Fringe" and "The League." She was also a suitcase model on "Deal or No Deal" before becoming a series regular as Rachel Zane in the legal drama "Suits." She filmed her final scenes in 2017 following her engagement, and her final episode aired in April 2018.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Of all the professional reinventions Meghan has attempted, acting makes the most sense," said Schofield. "She has legitimate experience doing it. She spent years working consistently on 'Suits.' There's nothing embarrassing about returning to the profession that originally made her successful."

"What I find amusing is the contradiction," she said. "Meghan spent years presenting herself as though acting was something she had evolved beyond. Perhaps the great reinvention is discovering that the original brand worked better than all the rebrands."

Stepping back in front of the camera could work in Meghan’s favor. Recent polls have placed both Harry and Meghan near the bottom of the royal family’s popularity rankings in Britain, ahead of only former Prince Andrew, People magazine reported.

But if there's one thing Meghan has consistently proven, it's her ability to command attention — the enduring power of the so-called "Markle Sparkle."

"Meghan brings something you cannot manufacture with a marketing budget, and that's global curiosity," said Schofield. "Love her or loathe her, people will watch the first episode just to see whether she can still act. Every photograph from the set becomes international news. Every trailer gets dissected. Every interview generates headlines."

"From a publicity standpoint, I completely understand why a producer might take that gamble," she said. "The question is whether the spectacle surrounding Meghan ultimately serves the story or overwhelms it. But there's an enormous difference between attracting attention and building a sustainable career. The real test is whether anybody wants to see Meghan's character again once the novelty wears off."

item.title: Dolly Parton's favorite Southern dishes, from chicken and dumplings to banana pudding
item.description: Country music star Dolly Parton's beloved Southern recipes included chicken and dumplings, buttermilk biscuits and gravy, banana pudding and her favorite chess pie.
item.content:encoded:
As the world mourns country music icon Dolly Parton following her death at age 80, her favorite Southern dishes offer a taste of the traditions she cherished throughout her life.

"We were born cooking, as they say," Parton told Food Network of growing up as one of 12 children in Tennessee. "All of my life, I remember being in the kitchen with somebody because life just centered around the kitchen."

Parton said she learned to cook from "all those wonderful relatives" she watched in the kitchen.

'GOLDEN GIRLS' KITCHEN COMES TO LIFE WITH CHEESECAKE AND '80S NOSTALGIA

"If I were giving you tips, I'd probably get a notice from the health department because I like to use a lot of butter," she told Food Network. "You've got to use a little bit of the things that really make things taste good if you're going after that soul food, so to speak. You've gotta use some grease — bacon grease, mainly."

The signature dishes Parton said she often prepared and liked to eat showcased her Southern roots. 

She published two cookbooks: "Dolly's Dixie Fixin's" in 2006 and, with her sister Rachel Parton George, "Good Lookin' Cookin'" in 2024.

Parton also endorsed several food and cooking products, including cake mixes and frozen meals, throughout her career.

FROM FONDUE TO CASSEROLES: CLASSIC 1960S FOODS THAT DEFINED A GENERATION

"I'm a really, really good cook," Parton told Wired in 2020. "I'm not a gourmet cook. My food is not pretty, but it's good."

Below are some of the Queen of Country Music's favorite foods.

A recipe for the Southern classic appeared in "Dollywood Presents: Tennessee Mountain Home Cooking," published in 1989. Decades later, Parton said in an interview with Country Living, "When I think about my mama, I think about some chicken and dumplings."

6 ICONIC AMERICAN RESTAURANTS STILL SERVING UP NOSTALGIA AND CLASSIC FLAVORS

"I like a good meatloaf. It's easy to make," she told the publication. "But I also love to make chicken and dumplings. I get a couple of chickens, and I get enough for everyone because everyone loves my chicken and dumplings!"

The 1989 recipe associated with Parton begins by simmering a whole chicken with onion and celery leaves in salted water, according to The Kitchn.

Parton said it would take her "all day" to make chicken and dumplings the way she liked them.

"I may read a while or try to relax while I check in on my cooking," she told Country Living. "It's the same thing with a meatloaf or fried chicken."

But Parton wouldn't give away all the details of her famous dish.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"I don't give out the recipe," she said. "Mine is all these secret ingredients — and the main one is love."

One of Parton's favorite breakfast foods was biscuits and gravy.

"Everybody makes biscuits, but how many people make buttermilk biscuits unless you really are from the South?" Parton said in a 2023 interview with Eater.

"I love it all. I eat gravy and biscuits at least once a week for breakfast with sausage or whatever. With the same pan, I'll get a biscuit and put apple butter or jam or jelly on there. Whatever looks good. There’s no bad way to eat a biscuit."

Parton described herself as more of a cook than a baker, but banana pudding was among her favorite desserts.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"Everybody loves banana pudding," she said on ABC's "Good Morning America" in 2022. "That was always one of my favorite things, a big old bowl of banana puddin'."

A recipe for the Southern staple, inspired by her mother's method, is included in "Dolly's Dixie Fixin's" and calls for a 12-ounce box of vanilla wafers and five to six sliced bananas.

Parton admitted to Wired that potatoes were her weakness.

"Every diet I ever fell off of has been because of a potato," Parton said. "Either french fries or mashed potatoes or baked potatoes. Potato, potato, potato! I never met a spud I didn't like."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Parton said a mayonnaise-based potato salad was her go-to dish to bring to a barbecue. She recalled that Sunday fried chicken served with potato salad was "one of the greatest things ever" from her childhood.

"When that happened at our church and that big bowl of potato salad got there, you didn't have to worry," she said during an interview on the "Today" show in 2022. "Even [if] it was sunny, it wasn't gonna last that long! It wasn't gonna go bad … not if I was around!"

Another love of Parton's was roast pork, "especially the fatty part," Parton said in a 1992 interview with The New York Times. "I can't help it. The greasier the food, the better."

Parton revealed to the Times in 1992 that one of her favorite meals to serve guests was roast pork with green beans, turnip greens and fried okra. 

Chess pie, a traditional Southern custard-style pie typically made with eggs, sugar, butter and flour or cornmeal, was Parton's favorite pie, she told USA Today in 2019.

"I don't eat much cake," she said. "I usually have pie on my birthday. My favorite pie is chess pie. That is 'chess,' not 'chest,' pie."

item.title: Strange Georgia crime-scene clues blow hole in theory of mom’s mysterious death, family says
item.description: Natalie Jones' toxicology report came back clean, yet Georgia authorities pushed an overdose theory before closing her 2020 Heard County death case.
item.content:encoded:
A negative toxicology report, missing teeth and an unusually positioned driver’s seat are fueling renewed questions into the unexplained 2020 death of Georgia mother Natalie Jones.

"The Truth About Natalie," a six-part Audiochuck series, examines the 27-year-old’s life before her disappearance, the circumstances surrounding her death and a questionable overdose theory.

The series draws from case files, crime-scene evidence, candid interviews with family members and a volunteer advocate, along with independent forensic analysis.

Jones’ mother, Elaine Gordon, told Fox News Digital that friction with investigators began during the search. She alleged that a detective accused her of interfering as she pressed for answers.

DETECTIVES' TRUE CRIME PODCAST TAKES FRESH SHOT AT KILLER WHO VANISHED AFTER CAUGHT-ON-CAMERA MURDER

"What did they expect me to do, sit at home and be quiet? And I still want somebody to answer this for me: How do we even know Natalie left that lake house in the first place?" Gordon told Fox News Digital.

Gordon also questioned whether investigators thoroughly interviewed everyone connected to her daughter’s final hours.

Jones disappeared after reportedly leaving a friend’s lake house in Jackson’s Gap, Alabama, on July 4, 2020, in a bright pink 2002 Chevrolet Cavalier. She planned to drive home to Heard County, Georgia.

At 12:52 a.m. the following morning, her phone sent its last outgoing text to the mother of a former boyfriend.

"I made it. Thanks."

The message did not indicate where Jones had arrived.

Cellphone data reviewed in the podcast indicated that on July 5, Jones’ phone connected with towers across Heard County in a scattered pattern, including on the opposite side of the county from her home. Cellular activity stopped shortly after 5 a.m.

Later that morning, Jones failed to arrive at her sister’s home to babysit her children, prompting the family to contact police.

Nearly three months passed without answers. Then, in October 2020, a property owner’s nephew discovered Jones’ vehicle off Roosterville Road in rural Heard County, covered in thick vegetation.

UC DAVIS FRATERNITY STUDENT'S 2001 DEATH RULED A SUICIDE AFTER 29 STAB WOUNDS QUESTIONED IN TRUE CRIME PODCAST

Heard County Sheriff’s Office deputies found Jones deceased in the driver’s seat, slumped toward the driver’s side door, wearing the same clothes she had worn to the gathering. Her body showed advanced decomposition and partial mummification.

The medical examiner could not determine Jones’ cause or manner of death.

GOLDEN STATE KILLER INVESTIGATOR FINDS ‘RED FLAGS’ IN MARILYN MONROE DEATH SCENE DECADES LATER

Although investigators said they found no evidence of foul play, the podcast highlighted several details that left Jones’ family scrambling for answers.

Crime-scene photos showed the driver’s seat reclined and pushed farther back than Jones, who stood 5 feet, 5 inches tall, would have kept it. Strands of her hair were wedged along the driver-side door jamb, and the vehicle’s trunk had been popped open.

Jones’ cellphone, rhinestone sandals, belt and white sunglasses were unaccounted for. Several of her teeth were also missing.

item.title: Macklin Celebrini explains why he didn't take Sharks to the cleaners with max contract
item.description: Macklin Celebrini left $2 million per year on the table in his $94 million extension to give the San Jose Sharks more salary cap flexibility.
item.content:encoded:
He may only be heading into his third NHL season, but San Jose Sharks star Macklin Celebrini is already on the cusp of being one of the league's highest-paid players by AAV ever.

The five-year, $94 million extension he signed this summer kicks in for the 2027-28 season and will see him making an AAV of $18.8 million per season.

Sharks GM Mike Grier was no doubt more than happy to pay this, but what's wild is that Celebrini left a nice chunk of change on the table.

SHARKS STAR MACKLIN CELEBRINI JUST MADE AN IMPRESSIVE BIT OF NHL AND VIDEO GAME HISTORY

According to Sportsnet, the most a player can be paid per season is 20% of the team's salary cap.

That meant Celebrini could've asked for $20.8 million per year, and the team probably would've done it. However, Celebrini is playing the long game to make sure the team is competitive in the years to come.

"I want to make sure that with where the (NHL salary) cap was going, that the number made sense for the team first and foremost," Celebrini said. "Making sure that everyone can get paid and that we're in a good spot to build the way we want to build, I felt like we kind of landed on that number.

"Keeping a little bit more flexibility for everyone, and I mean it's not really a bad thing. I'm committed to this team and this organization."

THE TALLEST PLAYER EVER SELECTED IN THE NHL BLEW MINDS IN HIS DEBUT WITH THE SAN JOSE SHARKS

That extra $2 million will certainly come in handy down the line, especially when the Sharks really start to get competitive again, and they will.

I don't think we're more than a few years away from the team being a big free agent destination again. They missed the playoffs by a few points last season, and with young stars like Celebrini, Will Smith, William Eklund, and Michael Misa, players will certainly be interested in signing.

The Sharks get their preseason underway on September 20 in Anaheim against a Ducks team that would kill for some cap flexibility right now, and then will open their regular season slate on October 1 at home against the Florida Panthers.

item.title: College football is back with all eyes on Bill Belichick as courtroom drama heats up

item.content:encoded:
Can you feel it? The temperature is starting to change, the leaves are slowly turning, and we have finally reached college football season — even if this weekend is only an appetizer.

The long seven-month offseason has been filled with congressional legislation, eligibility lawsuits, CFP expansion and plenty of other storylines that have distracted from the product on the field.

But don’t worry. When Bill Belichick leads North Carolina onto the field in Dublin, Ireland, for a matchup against TCU, it will signal that — at least for one day — all is right in the world.

MATT RHULE SOUNDS ALARM ON NFL RETURNEES, $45 MILLION ROSTERS AND COLLEGE FOOTBALL'S PAYROLL PROBLEM

If you can't get excited for Saturday, I don't know what to tell you.

Sure, it might not be the most intriguing slate of action, but it's also worth noting that you've likely spent the past seven months clamoring for the opportunity to dive back into your search for where exactly to watch these games.

As for North Carolina, the pressure is on Belichick to win this weekend. The Tar Heels cannot afford to come out of the gates looking anything like they did in last season's opener against the same team.

VIRGINIA CAVALIERS RELEASE WEEK ZERO INJURY REPORT FEATURING A SHOCKING NUMBER OF HURT PLAYERS

But don't you worry, we have plenty of other games this weekend to scratch that itch. Here's a look at the slate.

There’s your Saturday slate, with a few FCS matchups thrown into the mix.

So sit back and enjoy college football. And please, don’t complain about the appetizer we’re being given. You’ve been craving this since January.

Just because the season has officially started doesn’t mean the court system won’t dictate a number of athletes potentially seeing the field.

Right now, a battle is brewing in courtrooms in Texas and Louisiana involving college football players who have been granted the right to play this season by local judges.

The problem is that those court orders conflict with guidelines enacted by conferences such as the SEC and Big Ten.

How does this shake out?

On Friday, attorneys representing the athletes added the SEC to their amended lawsuits, which could force conference counsel to appear before a Louisiana judge in order to explain their reasoning behind not allowing an athlete to obey a legal order.

No, I wouldn’t expect SEC commissioner Greg Sankey to get within 100 miles of the Baton Rouge courtroom next week, but that doesn’t mean the situation won’t present problems if the judge were to grant the plaintiffs an injunction that allows them to play on Saturday.

GOVERNOR LANDRY BACKS LANE KIFFIN, LSU IN FIGHT WITH SEC: 'DON'T HATE THE PLAYER, HATE THE GAME'

If that were to happen, the SEC's next move is the one to watch.

Does the conference punish LSU under its new guidelines that schools are not allowed to play athletes who have professional ties? Would the SEC file some sort of lawsuit against the athletes to prevent them from playing?

Or, would Greg Sankey take aim at LSU specifically?

These are all questions that are going to present themselves over the next week, and there are plenty of other schools paying attention to what transpires in both Louisiana and Texas court rooms.

But, that can wait a few days. Finally, College Football has returned with a nice weekend slate to hold us over until next Thursday.

You earned it folks, because it's been one chaotic offseason.

Enjoy the day!

item.description: Over 9,000 bones remain unexamined at Fox Hollow Farm as the true crime documentary explores whether suspected serial killer Herb Baumeister acted alone.
item.content:encoded:
Nearly 30 years after thousands of human bones and bone fragments were unearthed at the sprawling estate of suspected serial killer Herb Baumeister, new questions are being raised about the mystery of what really happened at Fox Hollow Farm.

The coroner leading the renewed investigation claims a key figure in the case has not been fully forthcoming with investigators.

"I have had an opportunity to speak with Mark Goodyear a couple of times," Hamilton County Coroner Jeff Jellison told Fox News Digital.

FOX HOLLOW FARM SERIAL KILLER'S 10TH VICTIM IDENTIFIED: CORONER

"The first question I would ask him is, ‘Are you ready to be honest with me?’ Because in the conversations we’ve had, he’s not been honest. I’ve asked him questions that I knew the answer to, and he didn’t pass that test. So for me to sit down with Mark Goodyear, he’s going to have to be willing to be honest in this conversation. I don’t have time to sit down with somebody that tells lies, untruths."

Jellison appears in the ABC News Studios true crime documentary "Return to Fox Hollow: New Victims, Darker Secrets," which explores new theories about potential accomplices, overlooked evidence and witness accounts in the case of Baumeister, a suspected serial killer believed to have murdered numerous men in Indiana. It's a follow-up to the 2025 docuseries "The Fox Hollow Murders: Playground of a Serial Killer."

Jellison said he wants to determine whether Goodyear knows something that could help investigators identify the remaining victims and determine how they died.

Goodyear has never been charged with any crime related to the case and has repeatedly denied any involvement in the disappearances.

"If we move forward in that conversation, certainly I want to know any information I can gather to help identify these remains," said Jellison. "Were you familiar with anybody? Things that would focus more around identification and how these people died."

"Mark Goodyear knows a lot about this case," Jellison said.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Jellison also shared that Goodyear knew many people through gay nightclubs and could help investigators identify some of the remains.

Goodyear, who participated in the first docuseries, has described himself as Baumeister's only known survivor. The film detailed how investigators believed Baumeister may have filmed his victims with a secret camera hidden in an air vent in his basement. Goodyear said he was forced to watch some of the tapes in 1994. He said the video was so "bad" it made him scream.

"It was like having a camera right up against something," Goodyear said. "You're not going to be able to tell what's going on, but the minute you got a flash of what was going on, it made you scream."

The previous documentary examined how Goodyear's account of his relationship and encounters with Baumeister has changed over the years. At the time, Jellison told Fox News Digital it was unlikely those tapes, if they exist, would ever be recovered.

Fox News Digital reached out to Goodyear for comment but did not receive a response.

Goodyear initially agreed to another interview for the follow-up documentary but did not appear for the scheduled interview, according to the film.

About 10,000 burned and broken human bones and bone fragments were recovered from the 18-acre estate that once belonged to Baumeister. Before investigators could arrest him in 1996, Baumeister was found dead of a self-inflicted gunshot wound in Ontario, Canada. He was 49.

Investigators believe Baumeister frequented gay bars in Indianapolis, lured men to his home while his family was away, killed them there and disposed of their remains on the property.

Baumeister's son discovered a human skull in the woods at Fox Hollow Farm in 1994, but, according to reports, investigators did not search the property until June 1996.

Goodyear said he first encountered Baumeister at an Indianapolis gay bar in 1994, where Baumeister introduced himself as "Brian." Goodyear later told investigators that he went home with Baumeister and described what he said was a disturbing sexual encounter.

Goodyear's account eventually helped advance the investigation. After encountering Baumeister again the following year, Goodyear helped investigators obtain information that led them to identify Baumeister.

While Jellison has questioned Goodyear's account, he also made clear in the documentary that Goodyear was not a suspect.

GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB

"There are very strong indications there is another suspect, and it wasn’t Mark Goodyear," Jellison said in the film.

Jellison said there are still more than 9,000 bones and bone fragments yet to be examined. Investigators believe at least 25 people fell victim to Baumeister, according to WRTV.

The scope and placement of the remains have also raised another question for Jellison: whether Baumeister could have carried out the crimes alone.

"I was always convinced that there was more than one," Jellison said. "There were a lot of people that lost their lives in this incident, and just the placement of the evidence alone. How does one man pull this crime off? And how does one man get ... deceased individuals from his residence to potentially 200 yards through very dense woods? I think it would've been a very difficult task."

Jellison is determined to put names to the unidentified victims. He believes some families may still be unaware that a loved one vanished or that the person's remains may have ended up at Fox Hollow Farm.

Jellison compared the scale of the investigation to the recovery effort at the World Trade Center.

"Some of these folks did not have close family connections, and they were somewhat marginalized," he explained. "So there may be families out there not even knowing that their loved one went missing, much less consider that person was a victim at Fox Hollow."

"Thirty years have passed since these remains have been recovered," he reflected. "So potentially, mom and dad could be deceased, and maybe they had no brother or sister. So we’re reaching out further down the lineage to cousins. And a cousin may not even know that they had a family member that even went missing."

Jellison said identifying the Fox Hollow victims presents a unique challenge.

He contrasted the case with the World Trade Center investigation, where records and missing-person reports gave investigators a clearer idea of who they were looking for. At Fox Hollow, investigators started with remains but few clues about their identities.

"I really believe that this investigation is more complicated in some ways than the World Trade Center," he said. "With Fox Hollow, we’ve recovered these remains, but we have no idea who it is that we’re looking for."

Jellison is urging anyone who believes a missing loved one could be connected to the case to contact his office. After the original documentary aired, his office received approximately 500 emails, phone calls, text messages and social media messages, Jellison said.

item.title: Trump’s tougher round-two birthright citizenship strategy hinges on key legal distinction, experts say
item.description: President Donald Trump's new birthright citizenship orders target children of terrorists and foreign government employees using classic legal exceptions.
item.content:encoded:
Conservative legal experts say President Donald Trump’s latest attempts to narrow birthright citizenship and crack down on birth tourism may have stronger legal footing than his first effort.

After the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in June that children born in the United States to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present are citizens at birth under the 14th Amendment, Trump issued two new executive orders taking narrower approaches to citizenship and birth tourism.

The first, signed Aug. 6, directs federal agencies to withhold documents recognizing citizenship from certain children born when neither parent is a U.S. citizen, including some whose parents are members of designated foreign terrorist organizations, foreign-government employees or participants in transactions or fraud intended to obtain birthright citizenship.

Experts from the Manhattan Institute, America First Legal and the America First Policy Institute, all right-of-center organizations, argued that Trump’s new order is narrower than his first and is built around longstanding exceptions to birthright citizenship that they believe could apply here.

TRUMP SIGNS EXECUTIVE ORDERS TARGETING BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP, BIRTH TOURISM AFTER SUPREME COURT SETBACK

"The Supreme Court has long recognized that there are exceptions to the 14th Amendment's birthright citizenship clause for the aliens who are considered children of invading armies or the children of ambassadors," America First Policy Institute senior fellow Chad Mizelle, who previously served as the Justice Department’s chief of staff, told Fox News Digital. "So in a situation where you have a terrorist here contrary to the laws of the United States … who is looking to do harm … That has long been recognized by the Supreme Court, and basically going back to the history of our country, as recognized exceptions to any sort of claim of birthright citizenship."

United States v. Wong Kim Ark, decided by the Supreme Court in 1898, recognized exceptions to birthright citizenship for children of diplomats and children of alien enemies born during a hostile occupation. Trump’s order argues that members of foreign terrorist organizations can fall within that enemy exception.

TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP FIGHT COMES ROARING BACK WITH ‘INVADERS’ PLAY AFTER KAVANAUGH ROADMAP

"The Supreme Court ruled that you can't restrict birthright citizenship to kids of people in the country temporarily or illegally," Manhattan Institute director of constitutional studies Ilya Shapiro told Fox News Digital. "But what the new executive order does is it goes to one of the classic exceptions to birthrights citizenship, two of the classic exceptions, those who owe an allegiance to a foreign government, meaning employed by a foreign governing diplomats otherwise, and those who are invaders of foreign armies and terrorists, members of foreign organizations hostile to America, certainly qualify in that category."

David Bier, the director of immigration studies at the libertarian Cato Institute, however, argued that the president’s attempt to redefine what constitutes an alien enemy without going through Congress puts the administration on legally shaky ground.

"Congress ultimately establishes what it means to be subject to U.S. jurisdiction," Bier told Fox News Digital. "There's this very limited exception for accredited diplomats and everyone else in the United States is subject to U.S. laws so the idea that the president himself on his own authority can decide who is subject U. S. jurisdiction and U.S. laws is really a radical expansion and assertion of executive power and really would be unprecedented in the history of the United States."

JACKSON ACCUSES THOMAS OF ECHOING INFAMOUSLY RACIST COURT DECISION IN BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CLASH

"I really do think this case is testing a different proposition from the earlier case," Bier added, explaining that the issue at hand has more to do with executive power than birthright citizenship. "And I think it's a lot more questionable as well."

Amanda Frost, a professor at the University of Virginia School of Law, pointed out that United States v. Wong Kim Ark specifies that only children of enemies "occupying" some portion of the country are barred from citizenship at birth, meaning that Trump’s order would not apply to terrorists simply residing within the country. She said the Trump administration could potentially expand who is legally defined as a diplomat to preclude more people from birthright citizenship, but explained such a move would make it difficult to prosecute individuals for criminal offenses, a concern shared by Bier.

Frost and Bier both believe the new executive order should be ruled unconstitutional.

Some have floated the issue of standing as a potential problem for those looking to challenge Trump's order. Legal standing requires plaintiffs to show they suffered or imminently face a concrete injury caused by the defendant that a court can remedy.

"It's going to be interesting to see who actually does have standing to challenge this order," America First Legal co-founder and president Gene Hamilton told Fox News Digital. "Is there somebody who thinks that they're going to swept up in the definition of a foreign terrorist organization? And if so, it would be kind of fun to see them try to sue the government or have someone sue on their behalf."

Trump’s new order is already facing legal resistance.

TRUMP TO ASK SUPREME COURT TO REHEAR BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CASE AFTER 'INSANE DECISION'

The same groups who challenged his initial order are now arguing that his new one unlawfully creates exceptions to birthright citizenship that conflict with the Supreme Court’s June ruling. The order remains on the books but is not scheduled to take effect until Sept. 6, with a Maryland judge scheduled to hear an injunction request Aug. 28 and a related motion still pending in New Hampshire.

Issued on the same day as the first new executive order, the second order directed the State Department and the Department of Homeland Security to deny travel visas to or pursue removal actions against individuals believed to be in the country for the purposes of birth tourism. Birth tourism is a process through which noncitizens enter the United States while pregnant and give birth in order to secure citizenship for their child.

Hamilton described this second order as being on "sound, solid legal footing."

"It relies and invokes Section 215(a) of the INA to impose conditions and delegates authority of the Secretary of State … to ensure that we are not granting visas and allowing people to remain on visas who may be engaged in birth tourism," he explained. "It is the sovereign right and province of all governments across the world, and certainly the United States is no different, to determine who should be able to receive a visa and who shouldn't. There's no entitlement to a visa. There's no constitutional right to a visa."

SEN ERIC SCHMITT SEEKS TO END BIRTH TOURISM, REVOKE CITIZENSHIP FOR BABIES OF FOREIGN DIPLOMATS

Critics also argue that the administration already had tools to combat birth tourism. Since 2020, State Department rules have directed consular officers to deny visitor visas when they have reason to believe an applicant’s primary purpose is traveling to the United States to give birth and obtain citizenship for the child.

"No new executive orders are required for the federal government to go after birth tourism operators or deny fraudulent visa applications," Center for American Progress senior director of immigration policy Debu Gandhi told Fox News Digital. "Americans should take note that from day one, the Trump administration has tried to evade the Constitution's clear and unequivocal language on citizenship and unilaterally decide who is born an American."

If the administration’s latest effort fails, supporters of further limits on birthright citizenship could turn to Congress or pursue a constitutional amendment, which would require approval by three-fourths of the states.

Shapiro says that the administration is on "solid ground" but noted that "if they had proceeded originally in this more targeted, narrower way" then the Supreme Court may not have ruled against them originally.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Wednesday.

item.title: GOV JEFF LANDRY: SpaceX bets on Louisiana as America’s next frontier takes off in the South
item.description: Louisiana's governor says SpaceX's decision confirms the state's momentum after tax cuts, workforce training, and $250 billion in investments.
item.content:encoded:
For generations, Americans looked west when they thought about opportunity. Today, they should look south.

Louisiana has always powered America. We fueled the nation with energy, fed it through our farms and ports, built ships that defended it, and manufactured the products that helped it grow.

Now, we are helping lead America’s next frontier: space.

NASA AT 68: AMERICA MUST LEAD ON THE MOON, MARS AND BEYOND—OR CHINA WILL

With SpaceX choosing Louisiana for its newest chapter, our state is taking its place at the center of the economic and technological race that will define the 21st century. This is more than a win for Louisiana. It is a win for America.

For many years, Louisiana saw transformative investments land somewhere else. We watched other states attract the industries of the future while too many of our own left in search of opportunity.

Not anymore.

SpaceX did not choose Louisiana by accident.

THE RED-STATE WINNERS IN THE CLIMB TO BECOME AMERICA’S NEXT ECONOMIC POWERHOUSE

It chose Louisiana because we made a deliberate decision to compete.

Over the past two years, we have cut taxes, reduced bureaucracy, modernized economic development, strengthened workforce training, and created an environment where major employers know they can build and succeed.

THIS RED STATE HANDS REPUBLICANS FRESH AMMUNITION IN THE FIGHT OVER AMERICA'S ECONOMIC FUTURE

The results speak for themselves.

Louisiana has secured more than $250 billion in announced private investment. Meta is building one of the largest artificial intelligence data centers in history in North Louisiana. Hyundai Steel is investing billions in advanced manufacturing along our River. And Louisiana continues to solidify its position as America’s energy powerhouse through transformative LNG investments — including Woodside’s $17.5 billion Louisiana LNG project, Venture Global’s $18 billion expansion, and Commonwealth LNG’s $13 billion facility.

HOW AMERICAN ENERGY HELPED BUILD 250 YEARS OF FREEDOM AND OPPORTUNITY

Together, these projects are creating thousands of jobs, strengthening American energy security, and cementing Louisiana’s role as a global energy leader.

Louisiana is not betting its future on a single industry. We are building an economy that leads in energy, manufacturing, technology, and now aerospace.

INNOVATION IS KEY TO AMERICA STAYING A SUPERPOWER. BUT IT IS MISSING AN ESSENTIAL PIECE

SpaceX is the latest chapter in that story.

Some will see rockets. I see what they make possible.

ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM

I see high-paying jobs for Louisiana workers. I see engineers, welders, electricians, fabricators, software developers, and skilled tradespeople building the future right here. I see students who once believed they had to leave Louisiana to pursue careers in technology and innovation realizing they can build those careers at home. I see communities gaining investment, growth, and optimism. Most importantly, I see Louisiana becoming a state that attracts talent instead of exporting it.

That matters because the greatest challenge facing our state has never been a lack of resources. It has been a lack of opportunity.

For decades, Louisiana was known for what we were losing. Today, we are becoming known for what we are gaining.

The proof is already visible.

Louisiana recently recorded population growth for the second consecutive year. Young adults accounted for most of that growth. Our labor force participation rate recorded one of the largest increases in America as thousands more Louisianians entered or reentered the workforce.

People are choosing Louisiana again.

SpaceX did not create that momentum.

It confirms it.

This project joins a growing list of investments that send the same message to the country and the world: Louisiana is open for business, ready to compete, and prepared to win.

For too long, Louisiana was told to think smaller. We were told the industries of the future belonged somewhere else.

SpaceX proves otherwise.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The same state that helped America reach the moon through generations of aerospace manufacturing is now helping shape the future of space exploration itself. That should make every Louisianian proud.

More importantly, it should make every American optimistic.

Because when companies choose to build in Louisiana, they are choosing to build in America.

The future of American energy, artificial intelligence, manufacturing, and now space exploration is being written in places willing to compete for it. Louisiana is competing.

Louisiana is winning.

And if SpaceX’s decision proves anything, it is that America's next frontier runs straight through Louisiana.
